rules.name: Reverse shell in command line
rules.description: Matches classic interactive reverse-shell constructs in a command line — bash's /dev/tcp pseudo-device, `bash -i`, netcat with `-e`, or a mkfifo+nc/sh pipe. These hand an attacker an interactive shell back to their host and essentially never occur in legitimate software, so it's high-confidence.

rules.name: Download piped into a shell
rules.description: Flags `curl`/`wget` whose output is piped straight into a shell (the “curl | sh” pattern). It executes remote code with nothing written to disk and is the staple of droppers and one-line installers — treat unexpected hits as remote code execution.

rules.name: Base64-decoded payload piped to a shell
rules.description: Detects a base64-decoded blob piped into a shell — a standard way to smuggle and run an obfuscated payload past plain-text inspection (deobfuscation + execution). Legitimate use is rare.

rules.name: Reading the shadow password store
rules.description: Reading /etc/shadow (via cat/cp/grep/etc.) or running `unshadow` exposes the system's password hashes for offline cracking — a direct credential-access action with no benign interactive use.

rules.name: Credential-harvesting tool
rules.description: LaZagne, mimipenguin and 3snake are well-known open-source credential harvesters that scrape passwords from browsers, keyrings, and memory. Their presence on an endpoint is almost always malicious.

rules.name: Cloud credential file access
rules.description: A command line referencing cloud-credential files (~/.aws/credentials, ~/.config/gcloud, ~/.azure, ~/.oci, ~/.kube/config) indicates someone is reading long-lived cloud/cluster keys — a common pivot into cloud infrastructure. Keys on the credential path appearing in the command (e.g. cat/cp/grep).

rules.name: SSH private-key access
rules.description: Reading or copying a private SSH key (id_rsa/id_ed25519/…) via cat/cp/scp/tar/etc. is a precursor to lateral movement. Matches a file-handling command that references a private-key filename.

rules.name: Browser cookie / session theft
rules.description: Launching Chrome/Chromium with `--remote-debugging-port`, or touching the browser cookie store (Chrome `Cookies` DB / Firefox `cookies.sqlite`), targets live session cookies — used for session hijacking and MFA-bypass.

rules.name: SELinux set to permissive/disabled
rules.description: `setenforce 0` or editing SELINUX=disabled/permissive turns off SELinux mandatory access control. Disabling the LSM removes a core confinement layer and is a hallmark of defense evasion — high confidence.

rules.name: AppArmor disabled
rules.description: `aa-disable`/`aa-teardown` or masking the apparmor service turns off AppArmor confinement, letting profiled applications run unconstrained — a deliberate weakening of the system's MAC controls.

rules.name: Host firewall disabled / flushed
rules.description: Turning the host firewall off (`ufw disable`, `iptables -F`, `nft flush ruleset`, stopping firewalld) removes inbound connection filtering. Medium severity because some admin workflows legitimately do this.

rules.name: Security tool tampering (stop / kill EDR)
rules.description: Stopping, masking, or killing a known security agent (CrowdStrike/Falcon, SentinelOne, Wazuh, OSSEC, auditd, osquery, Falco/Tetragon, Defender/MDATP, Sophos, ESET…) via systemctl/service/pkill is defense evasion aimed at blinding monitoring — high confidence.

rules.name: Root CA certificate installed
rules.description: Copying a certificate into /usr/local/share/ca-certificates and running `update-ca-certificates` (or `trust anchor`) installs a new trusted root CA, letting an adversary transparently intercept TLS (adversary-in-the-middle) or trust malicious code. Legitimate installs are rare outside provisioning.

rules.name: Backups / snapshots destroyed
rules.description: Deleting Timeshift snapshots, btrfs subvolumes, or LVM snapshots removes the user's ability to recover files — a common precursor to ransomware or destructive attacks (inhibit system recovery).

rules.name: Immutable or setuid bit set
rules.description: Setting an immutable bit (`chattr +i`, to resist removal) or a setuid bit (`chmod u+s` / 4755) on a file is used to harden persistence or create a privilege-escalation path. Review what file is targeted.

rules.name: System logs cleared
rules.description: Vacuuming the journal (`journalctl --vacuum`) or removing/truncating /var/log/auth.log, syslog, or wtmp destroys forensic evidence (anti-forensics / defense evasion).

rules.name: Shell history logging disabled
rules.description: Disabling shell-history logging (unset HISTFILE, HISTSIZE=0, set +o history) is an anti-forensics step so the attacker's typed commands aren't recorded.

rules.name: Dynamic-linker preload tampering
rules.description: Writing to /etc/ld.so.preload or exporting LD_PRELOAD forces a library into other processes — the classic userland-rootkit / function-hooking technique used to hide files, processes, and network connections.

rules.name: File encryption via openssl (staging / ransomware)
rules.description: `openssl enc -e` encrypts files from the command line — used to stage/exfiltrate data and, when run broadly across a directory, as poor-man's ransomware. Review what is being encrypted.

rules.name: Screen capture utility
rules.description: scrot / grim / import (ImageMagick) / gnome-screenshot capture the screen. Low severity (often interactive), but scripted/automated use can indicate surveillance — confirm the requesting process.

rules.name: Tunneling / reverse-proxy tool
rules.description: cloudflared / ngrok / dev-tunnels and reverse SSH (`ssh -R`) expose the host or proxy C2 traffic out through an allowed service, bypassing inbound firewall rules — a common tunneling / C2 setup.

rules.name: Tor anonymizing proxy
rules.description: Running Tor (or a process opening a SocksPort) anonymizes outbound traffic, frequently to hide C2 or exfiltration destinations.

rules.name: rclone (cloud exfiltration tool)
rules.description: rclone syncs data to dozens of cloud providers and is frequently abused for bulk exfiltration to attacker-controlled storage.

rules.name: Adversary-in-the-middle proxy (mitmproxy)
rules.description: mitmproxy / mitmdump / mitmweb intercept and modify traffic (adversary-in-the-middle), used to capture credentials and tokens or inject content.

rules.name: Listener on a known-backdoor port
rules.description: A process listening on a port strongly associated with backdoors / C2 frameworks (4444 = Metasploit default, 1337/31337, 12345, …) suggests an implant awaiting inbound connections.

rules.name: Network port scanner (nmap)
rules.description: nmap performs active network/port scanning — internal reconnaissance to map reachable services, unusual on an endpoint outside admin or security work.

rules.name: Network packet sniffing
rules.description: tcpdump / tshark / dumpcap capture network traffic, used to harvest credentials or map the network.

rules.name: Security-software discovery
rules.description: Listing processes or units filtered for security products (CrowdStrike, SentinelOne, Wazuh, auditd, osquery, Falco…) is reconnaissance to identify what monitoring is present before evading it. Low severity — often benign admin activity.

rules.name: Virtualization / sandbox detection
rules.description: Querying systemd-detect-virt, dmidecode, or /sys/class/dmi for hypervisor / VM-vendor strings is sandbox evasion — malware checking whether it's under analysis before detonating.

rules.name: Root password / UID-0 manipulation
rules.description: Setting root's password (`passwd root`) or giving an account UID 0 (`usermod -u 0`, `useradd -o -u 0`) creates or unlocks root-equivalent access (privilege escalation / persistence).

rules.name: User added to a privileged group
rules.description: Adding an account to sudo/wheel/admin via usermod/gpasswd/adduser grants administrative rights — privilege escalation or backdoor-account setup.

rules.name: Sudoers NOPASSWD rule added
rules.description: Writing a NOPASSWD rule into /etc/sudoers or a /etc/sudoers.d/ drop-in grants passwordless root to an account — a stealthy privilege-escalation backdoor. High confidence.

rules.name: Local user created
rules.description: Creating a local account via useradd/adduser can establish a persistent backdoor login. Complements the account-baseline collector, which independently flags the resulting account.

rules.name: Local user deleted (account access removal)
rules.description: Deleting a local account (userdel / deluser) can be account-access removal — locking out a legitimate user or covering tracks.

rules.name: Cron job installed from stdin
rules.description: Piping into `crontab -` (or `crontab -` from stdin) installs a scheduled job without an editor — the scripted way malware adds cron persistence.

rules.name: Remote-access service enabled
rules.description: Enabling a remote-access service at boot (`systemctl enable ssh/xrdp/vnc`) opens an inbound entry point — valuable to an attacker for hands-on remote control.

rules.name: Kernel module loaded (possible rootkit)
rules.description: Loading a kernel module with insmod, or modprobe against a local .ko path, can install a rootkit or LKM backdoor operating in kernel space. Driver installs normally use modprobe by module name, so insmod and path-based modprobe stand out.

rules.name: UPX-packed executable
rules.description: UPX is a legitimate packer, but malware overwhelmingly uses it to shrink and obfuscate ELF payloads. Seeing upx invoked on-host is a strong obfuscation signal worth a look.

rules.name: Compiler building a binary on-host
rules.description: A compiler (gcc/cc/clang/tcc) building an output binary on the host is how droppers turn source into a native payload at runtime to evade file-based detection. Common on dev boxes, so it is low severity.

rules.name: Possible DNS-tunneled exfiltration
rules.description: DNS queries built from command substitution or from base64/xxd/od output are the shape of DNS tunneling — encoding stolen data into the labels of lookups to a name server the attacker controls.

rules.name: Archive piped to ssh/scp (exfil)
rules.description: An archive (tar/zip/gzip/openssl) piped into ssh, or an ssh command that tars a directory to stdout, is bulk collection funneled straight off-host over an encrypted channel.

rules.name: Password/encrypted archive of files
rules.description: Building a password-protected or encrypted archive (zip -p, gpg -c, openssl enc) is how collected data is bundled and hidden before exfil. Low severity since backups do it too.

rules.name: Clipboard access
rules.description: Reading the clipboard (xclip/xsel/wl-paste) can capture passwords and tokens a user copied. Low severity on its own, but meaningful alongside other collection activity.

rules.name: Password-policy discovery
rules.description: Enumerating the password policy (chage -l, passwd -S, /etc/login.defs, /etc/pam.d password config) tells an attacker how aggressively to attempt credential attacks. Discovery, so low severity.

rules.name: Browser bookmark/history access
rules.description: Accessing a browser's bookmarks or history store (Firefox places.sqlite, Chromium/Chrome History/Bookmarks) is reconnaissance of a user's sites and habits.

rules.name: System locale / region discovery
rules.description: Reading the system locale/timezone (localectl, timedatectl, bare `locale`, /etc/timezone) is commonly used by malware to fingerprint or geofence a target before acting. Discovery, low severity.

rules.name: Local group enumeration
rules.description: Enumerating local groups (getent group, reading /etc/group) maps privilege boundaries and admin membership — standard early-stage discovery.

rules.name: Local account enumeration
rules.description: Enumerating local accounts (getent passwd, reading /etc/passwd, lastlog, pinky) inventories who exists on the host and who has logged in — standard early-stage discovery.

rules.name: Destructive file/disk wipe
rules.description: Destructive wipes — shred, wipefs, dd over a raw disk device, or rm -rf against the filesystem root/--no-preserve-root — are impact actions that irreversibly destroy data. High confidence.

rules.name: Stopping or disabling services
rules.description: Stopping, disabling, masking, or killing services (systemctl/service stop, killall) is how attackers disable defenses, logging, or backups before impact.

rules.name: System shutdown or reboot
rules.description: Shutting down or rebooting the host (shutdown/reboot/poweroff/halt, init 0|6) can be a denial-of-service impact or a way to force a change to take effect. Admins do it too, so low severity.

rules.name: Shell startup-file persistence
rules.description: Appending to a shell startup file (~/.bashrc, ~/.profile, /etc/profile, /etc/profile.d) makes a command run at every login/shell — a classic, quiet persistence mechanism.

rules.name: Trap-based persistence
rules.description: A shell `trap` bound to EXIT/DEBUG/ERR re-runs a payload whenever the shell exits or before each command — an in-shell persistence and re-execution trick.

rules.name: PAM configuration modification
rules.description: Editing PAM configuration (/etc/pam.d) or dropping a pam_*.so module can backdoor authentication — silently accepting a password or capturing credentials at login. High confidence.

rules.name: Ad-hoc systemd execution
rules.description: systemd-run launches an arbitrary command as a transient systemd unit — a clean way to run or persist a payload as a managed service without editing unit files.

rules.name: Container escape attempt
rules.description: Container-escape primitives — nsenter into PID 1's namespaces, reaching /proc/1/root, capsh capability probing, or unshare --mount — are attempts to break out of a container onto the host. High confidence.

rules.name: Writing to process memory
rules.description: Referencing /proc/<pid>/mem or /proc/self/mem from a command line is process-memory tampering — reading secrets from or injecting code into a running process. High confidence.

rules.name: Kernel module / driver discovery
rules.description: Listing loaded kernel modules/drivers (lsmod, modinfo, /proc/modules) is reconnaissance of the kernel surface, often a precursor to loading a malicious module. Discovery, low severity.

rules.name: Systemd timer persistence
rules.description: Creating or enabling a systemd .timer (system or per-user) schedules recurring execution — the modern, cron-equivalent persistence path on systemd hosts.

rules.name: Job scheduled via at
rules.description: Scheduling a one-off job with `at` runs a command later, out of band from the current session — a lightweight scheduled-execution and persistence technique.

rules.name: Timestamp manipulation (timestomp)
rules.description: touch with -t/-r/-d or --date/--reference sets a file's timestamps to forge or match another file — timestomping to blend a dropped file into its surroundings and evade timeline analysis.

rules.name: Reading shell history (possible cred hunt)
rules.description: Reading a user's shell history (.bash_history/.zsh_history), especially grepping it, is a cheap hunt for passwords, tokens, and keys typed on the command line. Low severity discovery.

rules.name: Shell spawned by a browser or document app
rules.description: A shell or interpreter whose ANCESTRY includes a browser, mail client, or document viewer. Those applications open untrusted content; they have no legitimate reason to spawn a shell, so this is the classic exploitation / malicious-macro / drive-by chain. Lineage-based, so it fires regardless of what the command line says — renaming the payload doesn't help.

rules.name: Shell spawned by an internet-facing service (possible webshell/RCE)
rules.description: A shell or interpreter spawned by an internet-facing service (web server, app server, database). This is the signature of a webshell or successful remote code execution against that service, and is one of the highest-fidelity detections in existence — those daemons should never spawn shells. Covers the PHP web-worker set (php-fpm, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, LiteSpeed, and mod_php via apache), so a PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 / CVE-2026-109619) RCE that lands a shell is caught here. The Node runtime family (node, deno, bun) is covered too, so a Node2Shell (CVE-2026-111497) or any Node app RCE that spawns a shell is caught the same way.

rules.name: LiteLLM supply-chain C2 indicator in command line
rules.description: A command line referencing the litellm 1.107.0 supply-chain backdoor's indicators — its GitHub dead-drop (letters9813/pythonclient-test), the /codepy payload endpoint, the /tmp/remote_code_loader.lock marker, or the lookalike exfiltration domain www.litellm.dev. The backdoor runs in-process at Python startup, so the vulnerability finding and the advisory hunts are the primary coverage; this catches it when an indicator reaches a command line.

rules.name: LiteLLM supply-chain malware artifact on disk
rules.description: A file matching the litellm 1.107.0 backdoor's on-disk artifacts — the /tmp/remote_code_loader.lock daemon marker, or a cook.pth loader. Fires when such a path is under file monitoring; pair it with the advisory hunts to sweep site-packages and /tmp directly.

rules.name: Never-before-seen binary executing from a drop location
rules.description: A binary NEVER SEEN on this host before, executing from a temp / cache / Downloads / removable-media path. Rarity is the signal an adversary cannot fake — they can rename the file and rewrite the command line, but the first execution is still the first. Pairing novelty with a drop location is what keeps it precise: new binaries in /usr/bin are software updates; new binaries in /tmp are droppers.

rules.name: Command-and-control over a legitimate web service
rules.description: Command-and-control riding a legitimate web service — a Discord/Slack webhook, a Telegram bot API, a paste site, a raw GitHub script, or a one-shot file host. Commodity and AI-generated malware favour these because the destination is a trusted domain that egress filtering and reputation feeds allow.

rules.name: DNS-over-HTTPS resolver used from the command line
rules.description: A DNS-over-HTTPS resolver endpoint used straight from a command line. DoH hides name resolution from local DNS monitoring, so a script reaching one directly is usually evading inspection rather than browsing.

rules.name: AI coding agent performing a high-risk action
rules.description: An AI coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, aider, Cline, …) whose child process performs a high-risk action — piping a download into a shell, reading /etc/shadow or SSH private keys, or escalating. These agents execute shell commands with the user's full privileges, so a prompt-injected or hijacked agent is remote code execution that otherwise looks exactly like normal developer activity. Scoped to dangerous actions so ordinary agent work (builds, installs, tests) stays quiet.

rules.name: AI tool/MCP configuration modified from the command line
rules.description: An MCP server / AI tool configuration being WRITTEN from a command line. An MCP server runs locally with your privileges, so silently registering one is the AI-era equivalent of a malicious package or browser extension — persistent, privileged, and rarely reviewed. Reading these files does not alert.

rules.name: AI provider API key targeted
rules.description: A command line referencing an AI provider API key variable. These keys are high value, usually sit in plaintext in .env files, shell profiles, and tool configs, and are rarely rotated — an attractive, low-friction credential-theft target that traditional credential rules miss entirely.

rules.name: File uploaded to an AI API endpoint
rules.description: A file being UPLOADED to an AI provider API endpoint (curl -F file=@ / --data-binary @ / --upload-file). Model APIs are a new egress channel that looks benign to network monitoring: TLS to a reputable, allow-listed domain. Ordinary inline API calls do not match — only file uploads do.

rules.name: Local LLM runtime listening on a public interface
rules.description: A local LLM runtime (Ollama and friends) listening on a wildcard interface instead of loopback. That exposes an unauthenticated model server — and often the host's files and tools — to anyone on the network. A misconfiguration far more than an attack, which is exactly why it goes unnoticed.

rules.name: Hidden local account
rules.description: A local account flagged hidden — excluded from the login window and from casual enumeration. Legitimate service accounts are created by installers with known identifiers; a hidden account appearing on a workstation is a classic persistence backdoor.

rules.name: Non-root account with uid 0
rules.description: An account other than root carrying uid 0. Unix authorises on the numeric uid, not the name, so this is a full root backdoor wearing an innocuous username. There is no benign reason for it.

rules.name: Scheduled job runs from a drop location
rules.description: A scheduled job (launchd / cron / systemd) whose program lives in a temp, cache, Downloads, hidden or removable-media path. Persistence is only useful if it points at a payload, and legitimate software installs its payload somewhere durable — not /tmp.

rules.name: Scheduled job downloads and executes
rules.description: A scheduled job whose command downloads and pipes straight into a shell, or decodes base64 into one. That is persistence and staging in a single line: every execution re-fetches whatever the operator is serving, so the payload can change without touching the host again.

rules.name: Scheduled job masquerades as a system component
rules.description: A scheduled job named after a system component but whose program is NOT a system binary. Real platform jobs run platform binaries; borrowing the name while pointing elsewhere is deliberate blending, and the name/target mismatch is what gives it away.

rules.name: Security control disabled (host state)
rules.description: A security control reported as disabled by the host-state collector. This is the state-based counterpart to the command-line rules that catch the act of disabling it — so the finding survives even if the tampering happened before Scouter was installed, or off-host.

rules.name: Remote-access service enabled (host state)
rules.description: An inbound remote-access service is enabled. Often deliberate, but it is an entry point that should be a known decision rather than a surprise — and attackers enable these to keep a hands-on channel.

rules.name: Persistence file created or replaced
rules.description: A persistence file (launch agent/daemon, cron entry, systemd unit, init script) created or replaced, seen by the REAL-TIME FILE SENSOR rather than by a command line. This is an independent route to the same techniques the command-line persistence rules cover: reword the command, use a different tool, or write the file from a compiled binary and this still fires, because it watches the OUTCOME rather than the phrasing.

rules.name: Shell startup file created or replaced
rules.description: A shell startup file created or replaced. Same independence argument as the persistence-file rule — the command-line rule catches `echo ... >> ~/.zshrc`, this catches the file changing no matter how it was done.

rules.name: SSH authorized_keys created or replaced
rules.description: An SSH authorized_keys file created or replaced — the quietest durable backdoor there is, because it needs no malware and survives password changes.

rules.name: Log or audit file deleted
rules.description: A log, audit or shell-history file deleted. Logs are removed to destroy the record of what happened; catching the deletion itself is independent of whatever command performed it.

rules.name: /etc/ld.so.preload created or modified (preload rootkit)
rules.description: /etc/ld.so.preload forces a library into every dynamically linked process; QLNX injects its PAM backdoor this way. Writing this file is close to definitional for a userland rootkit.

rules.name: /etc/ld.so.preload present on disk
rules.description: The mere presence of /etc/ld.so.preload is worth a look: most estates never use it, and preload rootkits depend on it.

rules.name: PAM module written outside package management (PAM backdoor)
rules.description: A PAM module appearing outside package management means authentication itself has been modified. QLNX's PAM backdoor logs plaintext credentials as users log in.

rules.name: Hidden credential log in /var/log (.ICE-unix pattern)
rules.description: QLNX writes XOR-encrypted harvested credentials to /var/log/.ICE-unix, a name chosen to resemble an X11 socket directory. Hidden files under /var/log are not a normal packaging artefact.

rules.name: Shared object compiled on the host from an inline source string
rules.description: QLNX carries its rootkit as embedded C source and compiles it on the victim with the host's own gcc, so no malicious binary crosses the network. A -shared -fPIC build referencing dlsym or RTLD_NEXT from a temp directory is that pattern.

rules.name: eBPF program loaded by a non-observability process
rules.description: eBPF is increasingly used to hide processes, files and ports from ps, ls and netstat. QLNX and VoidLink both ship eBPF components, and bpf_probe_write_user or bpf_override_return have essentially no benign use outside tracing research.

rules.name: XDG autostart entry written outside a package install
rules.description: XDG autostart runs at desktop login and is often missed by sweeps that only check services and cron. QLNX uses it alongside systemd.

rules.name: Shell profile appended with a launcher
rules.description: Appending a downloader or reverse shell to a shell profile survives reboots and needs no privileges — common to QLNX and most commodity Linux implants.

rules.name: SSH private keys collected in bulk
rules.description: Bulk collection of SSH private keys turns one compromised developer workstation into access across the estate. QLNX harvests keys, cloud configs and shell history together.

rules.name: System logs truncated or wiped
rules.description: Truncating wtmp, btmp, lastlog or auth.log, or vacuuming the journal to nothing, destroys the record of how access was obtained. QLNX wipes logs as a routine step.

rules.name: Remote-management agent (RMM) installed or started
rules.description: A commercial remote-management tool starting on an endpoint. These are legitimate, signed products, so nothing else flags them — which is why intrusion sets install one instead of a RAT (the SMOKE#SCREEN campaign pairs ScreenConnect with Cloudflare tunnels). Benign where the customer's own IT uses one, so suppress the sanctioned product per site rather than the whole rule.

rules.name: udev rule that executes a program
rules.description: A udev rule carrying RUN+= executes a program whenever a matching device event fires — persistence that survives reboot, runs as root, and is missed entirely by a sweep that only looks at systemd units and cron.

rules.name: rc.local or SysV init script modified
rules.description: /etc/rc.local and the SysV init scripts still run on most distributions and are a standard place to hide a launcher, precisely because modern tooling looks at systemd instead.

rules.name: update-motd.d script modified
rules.description: Scripts in /etc/update-motd.d run as root on each interactive SSH login. Persistence there executes every time an administrator connects, which also makes it self-triggering.

rules.name: Kernel module written or installed outside package management
rules.description: A kernel module appearing outside package management, or loaded from a temporary or home directory. VoidLink's C2 compiles a rootkit module on demand for each target's exact kernel version, which defeats hash-based detection but still requires the module to land on disk and be loaded.

rules.name: sshd binary or an sshd-linked library replaced
rules.description: Replacing sshd or a library it links (libkeyutils is the classic) backdoors authentication itself, capturing every credential used to log in. ELF/Sshdinjector is the family that made this routine; nothing legitimate overwrites sshd outside a package upgrade.

sql_rules.name: Mass file rewriting (ransomware pattern)
sql_rules.description: One process creating or renaming 60+ files inside five minutes. Encryption-for-impact does not look like a command line — it looks like a storm of file rewrites — so this watches the shape of the activity instead. The five-minute bucket and single-actor grouping are what separate a ransomware run from a compiler or a backup, which touch just as many files but spread out and from a known toolchain.
sql_rules.sql:
SELECT actor, COUNT(*) AS files_touched, COUNT(DISTINCT path) AS distinct_paths,
 MIN(path) AS example_path,
 datetime(MIN(ts),'unixepoch','localtime') AS started,
 datetime(MAX(ts),'unixepoch','localtime') AS ended
FROM file_events
WHERE ts >= CAST(strftime('%s','now') AS INTEGER) - 86400
 AND event IN ('create','rename') AND actor IS NOT NULL AND actor != ''
GROUP BY actor, ts / 300
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 60 AND MAX(ts) - MIN(ts) <= 300
ORDER BY files_touched DESC LIMIT 25

sql_rules.name: Mass file deletion (wiper pattern)
sql_rules.description: One process deleting 60+ files inside five minutes — destruction observed as an outcome rather than inferred from an `rm` command line, so it holds regardless of the tool used.
sql_rules.sql:
SELECT actor, COUNT(*) AS files_deleted, MIN(path) AS example_path,
 datetime(MIN(ts),'unixepoch','localtime') AS started,
 datetime(MAX(ts),'unixepoch','localtime') AS ended
FROM file_events
WHERE ts >= CAST(strftime('%s','now') AS INTEGER) - 86400
 AND event = 'unlink' AND actor IS NOT NULL AND actor != ''
GROUP BY actor, ts / 300
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 60 AND MAX(ts) - MIN(ts) <= 300
ORDER BY files_deleted DESC LIMIT 25

sql_rules.name: Repeated authentication failures (brute force)
sql_rules.description: Counts failed authentications per user in a rolling window. A single failure is a typo; a burst is an attack, and no single event can express that — this is a question only correlation can answer, which is why it lives here rather than in a node rule. A success immediately following the burst is reported alongside, because that is the difference between a repelled attempt and a breach.
sql_rules.sql:
WITH fails AS (
 SELECT user, source, ts FROM auth_events
 WHERE success = 0 AND ts >= CAST(strftime('%s','now') AS INTEGER) - 86400)
SELECT f.user, COUNT(*) AS failures,
 (SELECT GROUP_CONCAT(DISTINCT s2.source) FROM fails s2 WHERE s2.user = f.user) AS sources,
 datetime(MIN(f.ts),'unixepoch','localtime') AS first_failure,
 datetime(MAX(f.ts),'unixepoch','localtime') AS last_failure,
 (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM auth_events s WHERE s.success = 1 AND s.user = f.user
    AND s.ts BETWEEN MIN(f.ts) AND MAX(f.ts) + 300) AS succeeded_after
FROM fails f GROUP BY f.user
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 8 AND MAX(f.ts) - MIN(f.ts) <= 3600
ORDER BY failures DESC LIMIT 25

sql_rules.name: Successful remote login from a never-before-seen source
sql_rules.description: A successful remote authentication from a source address this host has never accepted a login from before. Valid credentials used from a new place is what account compromise looks like from the endpoint — there is no malware to find, which is exactly why novelty is the only available signal.
sql_rules.sql:
WITH known AS (
 SELECT DISTINCT source FROM auth_events
 WHERE success = 1 AND ts < CAST(strftime('%s','now') AS INTEGER) - 86400)
SELECT datetime(a.ts,'unixepoch','localtime') AS at, a.user, a.source, a.method, a.etype
FROM auth_events a
WHERE a.success = 1 AND a.ts >= CAST(strftime('%s','now') AS INTEGER) - 86400
 AND a.source IS NOT NULL AND a.source != '' AND a.source != 'console'
 AND a.source NOT IN (SELECT source FROM known)
ORDER BY a.ts DESC LIMIT 25

sql_rules.name: Beaconing — regular check-in to one destination
sql_rules.description: Finds command-and-control by its RHYTHM rather than its content. Malware has to check in; that check-in is periodic, and periodicity is something an implant cannot hide by renaming itself or encrypting its traffic. Intervals come from the edge-triggered connection log (a connection is recorded when it APPEARS, so a beacon that reconnects on a timer leaves one row per beat), and regularity is scored as the squared coefficient of variation of those intervals — below 0.05 catches beacons jittered up to ~30%, which covers the usual C2 defaults. Three gates keep it quiet: the destination must be NEW to this host (first seen within 14 days), which removes the steady-state legitimate pollers that beacon perfectly (Slack, Dropbox, update checkers); it must be contacted by fewer than three distinct executables, which removes shared CDNs; and it needs at least 8 beats over at least 30 minutes. Thresholds are worth tuning to your environment — raise the jitter bound to catch sloppier beacons at the cost of noise.
sql_rules.sql:
WITH ev AS (
 SELECT exe, proc_name, raddr, rport, asorg, country, ts,
        ts - LAG(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY exe, raddr ORDER BY ts) AS gap
 FROM conn_events WHERE ts >= CAST(strftime('%s','now') AS INTEGER) - 86400),
agg AS (
 SELECT exe, proc_name, raddr, rport, asorg, country,
        COUNT(*) AS beats, AVG(gap) AS mean_gap, MIN(ts) AS t0, MAX(ts) AS t1,
        (AVG(gap*gap) - AVG(gap)*AVG(gap)) AS var_gap
 FROM ev WHERE gap IS NOT NULL AND gap > 0 GROUP BY exe, raddr),
novel AS (
 SELECT raddr FROM connections WHERE public=1 AND raddr IS NOT NULL
 GROUP BY raddr HAVING MIN(first_seen) >= CAST(strftime('%s','now') AS INTEGER) - 1209600)
SELECT a.proc_name, a.exe, a.raddr, a.rport, a.asorg, a.country,
 a.beats, CAST(a.mean_gap AS INTEGER) AS mean_gap_s,
 ROUND(CASE WHEN a.mean_gap > 0 THEN (a.var_gap / (a.mean_gap*a.mean_gap)) ELSE 9 END, 3) AS jitter,
 datetime(a.t0,'unixepoch','localtime') AS first_beat,
 datetime(a.t1,'unixepoch','localtime') AS last_beat
FROM agg a JOIN novel n ON n.raddr = a.raddr
WHERE a.beats >= 8 AND a.mean_gap >= 45 AND a.t1 - a.t0 >= 1800
 AND a.var_gap IS NOT NULL
 AND (a.var_gap / (a.mean_gap*a.mean_gap)) < 0.05
 AND a.raddr NOT IN (SELECT raddr FROM conn_events GROUP BY raddr HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT exe) >= 3)
ORDER BY jitter ASC, a.beats DESC LIMIT 25

sql_rules.name: Downloaded file executed
sql_rules.description: Correlates the downloads table against process executions: a file that arrived from the internet and then RAN within 24 hours. This is how ordinary people actually get compromised — the fake installer, the trojanised updater, the 'codec' from a search ad — and neither half looks alarming alone.
sql_rules.sql:
SELECT d.name AS downloaded, d.source_url, p.exe AS executed, p.cmdline,
 datetime(d.first_seen,'unixepoch','localtime') AS downloaded_at,
 datetime(p.first_seen,'unixepoch','localtime') AS executed_at
FROM downloads d JOIN processes p ON (p.exe = d.path OR p.exe LIKE '%/' || d.name)
WHERE p.first_seen >= d.first_seen AND p.first_seen - d.first_seen <= 86400
 AND d.first_seen >= CAST(strftime('%s','now') AS INTEGER) - 604800
ORDER BY p.first_seen DESC LIMIT 25

sql_rules.name: Newly dropped binary contacted the internet
sql_rules.description: A binary first seen within the last day, living in a temp / cache / Downloads / removable path, that opened an outbound internet connection within ten minutes of first running. Dropper lands, dropper phones home. The location filter is what keeps it precise — legitimate software updates land in /usr and /Applications.
sql_rules.sql:
SELECT p.name, p.exe, c.raddr, c.rport, c.country, c.asorg,
 datetime(p.first_seen,'unixepoch','localtime') AS first_run,
 datetime(c.first_seen,'unixepoch','localtime') AS first_contact
FROM processes p JOIN connections c ON c.exe = p.exe
WHERE c.direction='outbound' AND c.public=1
 AND c.first_seen >= p.first_seen AND c.first_seen - p.first_seen <= 600
 AND p.first_seen >= CAST(strftime('%s','now') AS INTEGER) - 86400 AND (p.exe LIKE '/tmp/%' OR p.exe LIKE '/private/tmp/%' OR p.exe LIKE '/var/tmp/%' OR p.exe LIKE '/dev/shm/%' OR p.exe LIKE '%/Downloads/%' OR p.exe LIKE '%/.cache/%' OR p.exe LIKE '/Volumes/%' OR p.exe LIKE '/run/user/%')
ORDER BY p.first_seen DESC LIMIT 25

sql_rules.name: Discovery burst followed by credential access
sql_rules.description: Three or more discovery commands (whoami / uname / netstat / ps / passwd enumeration) inside ten minutes, followed by a credential-access command. Each command is individually unremarkable — admins run all of them — but the SEQUENCE is the signature of hands-on-keyboard reconnaissance turning into theft.
sql_rules.sql:
WITH disco AS (SELECT ts FROM exec_events WHERE ts >= CAST(strftime('%s','now') AS INTEGER) - 86400 AND (cmdline LIKE '%whoami%' OR cmdline LIKE '%uname -a%' OR cmdline LIKE '%netstat%' OR cmdline LIKE '%ifconfig%' OR cmdline LIKE '%ps aux%' OR cmdline LIKE '%/etc/passwd%' OR cmdline LIKE '%getent%' OR cmdline LIKE '%arp -a%' OR cmdline LIKE '%lsof %'))
SELECT datetime(e.ts,'unixepoch','localtime') AS at, e.exe, e.cmdline,
 (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM disco d WHERE d.ts BETWEEN e.ts - 600 AND e.ts) AS discovery_cmds_before
FROM exec_events e
WHERE e.ts >= CAST(strftime('%s','now') AS INTEGER) - 86400 AND (e.cmdline LIKE '%/etc/shadow%' OR e.cmdline LIKE '%.ssh/id_%' OR e.cmdline LIKE '%keychain%' OR e.cmdline LIKE '%find-generic-password%' OR e.cmdline LIKE '%.aws/credentials%' OR e.cmdline LIKE '%API_KEY%' OR e.cmdline LIKE '%bash_history%')
 AND (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM disco d WHERE d.ts BETWEEN e.ts - 600 AND e.ts) >= 3
ORDER BY e.ts DESC LIMIT 25

sql_rules.name: Credential access followed by outbound transfer
sql_rules.description: A credential-access command followed within fifteen minutes by an outbound connection to the public internet. Steal, then send. The highest-severity chain here because it captures the moment an intrusion becomes a breach.
sql_rules.sql:
WITH cred AS (SELECT e.ts, e.exe, e.cmdline FROM exec_events e WHERE e.ts >= CAST(strftime('%s','now') AS INTEGER) - 86400 AND (e.cmdline LIKE '%/etc/shadow%' OR e.cmdline LIKE '%.ssh/id_%' OR e.cmdline LIKE '%keychain%' OR e.cmdline LIKE '%find-generic-password%' OR e.cmdline LIKE '%.aws/credentials%' OR e.cmdline LIKE '%API_KEY%' OR e.cmdline LIKE '%bash_history%'))
SELECT datetime(cr.ts,'unixepoch','localtime') AS credential_access_at, cr.cmdline AS credential_cmd,
 c.proc_name AS egress_proc, c.raddr, c.rport, c.asorg,
 datetime(c.first_seen,'unixepoch','localtime') AS egress_at
FROM cred cr JOIN connections c
 ON c.direction='outbound' AND c.public=1 AND c.first_seen BETWEEN cr.ts AND cr.ts + 900
ORDER BY cr.ts DESC LIMIT 25

sql_rules.name: Persistence established right after a flagged execution
sql_rules.description: A persistence mechanism (launchd / cron / systemd job) created within fifteen minutes of a high or critical severity process running. Attackers establish persistence immediately after gaining execution; this ties the foothold to the payload that created it.
sql_rules.sql:
SELECT j.kind, j.label, j.program, datetime(j.first_seen,'unixepoch','localtime') AS persisted_at,
 p.name AS preceding_process, p.severity AS process_severity, p.cmdline
FROM jobs j JOIN processes p ON p.first_seen BETWEEN j.first_seen - 900 AND j.first_seen
WHERE j.first_seen >= CAST(strftime('%s','now') AS INTEGER) - 86400 AND p.severity IN ('high','critical')
ORDER BY j.first_seen DESC LIMIT 25

sql_rules.name: Remote login followed by hands-on-keyboard activity
sql_rules.description: A successful remote login followed inside thirty minutes by three or more suspicious commands (credential paths, downloads, chmod +x, base64). Remote administration is normal; remote administration that immediately starts pulling tooling and reading secrets is not — this is the server-side counterpart to the workstation SSH rule.
sql_rules.sql:
WITH logins AS (SELECT ts, user, source FROM auth_events
 WHERE success=1 AND ts >= CAST(strftime('%s','now') AS INTEGER) - 86400
  AND (etype LIKE '%ssh%' OR method LIKE '%ssh%' OR message LIKE '%sshd%'))
SELECT datetime(l.ts,'unixepoch','localtime') AS login_at, l.user, l.source,
 COUNT(e.id) AS suspicious_cmds
FROM logins l JOIN exec_events e ON e.ts BETWEEN l.ts AND l.ts + 1800
WHERE (e.cmdline LIKE '%/etc/shadow%' OR e.cmdline LIKE '%.ssh/id_%' OR e.cmdline LIKE '%wget %'
 OR e.cmdline LIKE '%curl %' OR e.cmdline LIKE '%base64 %' OR e.cmdline LIKE '%chmod +x%')
GROUP BY l.ts, l.user, l.source HAVING COUNT(e.id) >= 3
ORDER BY l.ts DESC LIMIT 25
